solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: One goes without rasher

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a person who abstains from food
second meaning: more rash, i.e. quicker to act without thought

explanation.walkthrough: 'Rasher' tempts you towards bacon, but here it is the comparative of rash; 'One goes without' describes someone keeping a fast.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone observing a fast abstains from eating, and a more hasty or reckless action is quicker, so both senses meet in one word.

clue.text: Beware supporting cheat — one goes in pockets

indicators.note: in a down entry, a support sits underneath, so the preceding word's piece goes below the next

parts.note: to fob someone off is to cheat or trick them
as in 'watch out'

explanation.surface: A warning that a swindler is about, and someone's wallet is going into pockets.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, 'supporting' means sitting underneath, so the 'Beware' word goes below the 'cheat' word.
explanation.definitionFit: A traditional timepiece on a chain, designed to be carried in a small waistcoat pocket rather than worn on the wrist.

clue.text: Ultimately this medicine said to be best is worst

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter of the following word is kept

parts.note: final letter of the word
the proverb says laughter is the best medicine

explanation.surface: A remark that some remedy is supposedly the best but is actually the worst.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Worst' is not the superlative of bad but a verb meaning to defeat, which is the sense the definition needs.
explanation.definitionFit: To worst an opponent is to beat them, and to slaughter them is to beat them overwhelmingly, so both are verbs of defeat.

clue.text: Whirl lingerie with top off

indicators.note: removing the top of a word in a down entry drops its first letter

parts.note: a teddy is a one-piece undergarment

explanation.surface: Someone twirls about in their underwear having taken their top off.
explanation.walkthrough: A teddy is a woman's one-piece item of lingerie; losing its first letter leaves the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A small swirling current of water or air spins round, so it is a whirl in the noun sense.

clue.text: Castle is mostly plain and honest

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the last letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: bald means plain or unadorned, as in a bald statement; its last letter goes
upright, honest

explanation.surface: A description of a castle as fairly simple and straightforward.
explanation.walkthrough: BALMORAL is the British royal family's castle in the Scottish Highlands.
explanation.definitionFit: Balmoral is a specific example of a castle, the Scottish royal residence in Aberdeenshire.

clue.text: Declare weather to be ordinary

parts.note: to aver is to state firmly
weather as a verb means to wear or age, as weathered stone

explanation.surface: A forecaster announces that the weather will be nothing special.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Weather' reads as a noun but works as a verb meaning to be worn down by time.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unremarkable and typical sits in the middle of the range, so the adjective is a synonym.

clue.text: JP from Margate is otherwise tense inside

indicators.note: something put inside goes into the middle of the rest
otherwise means in a different way, so the letters are arranged differently

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
T is the grammar abbreviation for tense

explanation.surface: A justice of the peace from the Kent seaside town of Margate is on edge.
explanation.walkthrough: Margate is an English seaside resort; 'tense' looks like an adjective about the JP's nerves but supplies a grammar abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: A Justice of the Peace is a lay judge in the lower courts, which in Britain is the same office as a magistrate.

clue.text: Drink causing endless debauchery, yes for German

indicators.note: without an end means the final letter is cut away

parts.note: a riot is wild revelry, as in running riot; its last letter goes
the German word for yes

explanation.surface: A drink so potent it leads to non-stop revelry, with a German happily agreeing.
explanation.walkthrough: A riot can mean an unrestrained bout of revelry, which is how it fits 'debauchery'.
explanation.definitionFit: Rioja is a Spanish red wine from the region of the same name, so it is an example of an alcoholic beverage.

clue.text: Get a load of lean English sirloin from the back

parts.note: a ship that lists leans to one side
standard abbreviation

indicators.note: taking from the back means picking the final letter

parts.note: final letter of the cut of beef

explanation.surface: Admire a big portion of lean English beef cut from the rear of the animal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lean' is not a description of the meat but a verb, as a ship leans.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Get a load of this' is a colloquial command to pay attention, which is what hearing carefully means in speech.

clue.text: Counters reports about bishop

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece is wrapped round another

parts.note: accounts or stories
chess notation for bishop

explanation.surface: A churchman's critic rebuts stories about a bishop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Counters' is read as a verb in the surface, but the definition is the plural noun for flat surfaces.
explanation.definitionFit: Shop counters and tables are both flat raised surfaces for laying things on, so the plural nouns are near synonyms.

clue.text: Enter being up for backgammon, say

parts.note: to board a ship or train is to get on it
game means willing, as in up for it

explanation.surface: Someone signing up for a backgammon tournament.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' marks backgammon as an example of the answer rather than a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: Backgammon is played with counters on a marked surface, making it one instance of the tabletop pastime category.

clue.text: Grand defeat leads to misleading explanation

parts.note: G is slang shorthand for a grand, a thousand
a beating

explanation.surface: A big loss is followed by a spin-doctor's misleading account of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grand' looks like an adjective describing the defeat but gives a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To put a gloss on events is to give a superficially attractive interpretation that hides the truth.

clue.text: First boat in the past to carry king

indicators.note: carrying something means holding it inside

parts.note: as in 'years ago'
R for Rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: An early vessel from long ago that once transported a monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: A nod to the setter's own pseudonym, Jason, whose ship it was in Greek myth.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek legend Jason's ship carrying the Argonauts is often called the first ever built, hence earliest vessel.

clue.text: Decent pan gives a chance to start again

parts.note: decent, inoffensive, as clean jokes
to pan or slate is to criticise harshly

explanation.surface: A decent saucepan lets a cook begin afresh.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pan' looks like kitchenware but is the verb meaning to review badly; slate in this sense is British.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom comes from wiping a schoolroom writing tablet, meaning past errors are forgotten and a fresh start is possible.

clue.text: Jack to match child's habit

parts.note: a jack or jack tar is a seaman
to suit is to go well with

explanation.surface: A boy called Jack copying a younger child's routine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Habit' is not a routine but clothing, as in a riding habit or a nun's habit.
explanation.definitionFit: Children were traditionally dressed in naval-style outfits with wide collars, so this is a garment typically worn by the young.

clue.text: What filibusters wield is suspended by girl

parts.note: a service cut off is suspended
a young woman

explanation.surface: A parliamentary debate tactic is halted by a young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: Filibusters today means politicians talking out a bill, but its older sense is freebooters or pirates; 'by' simply places one piece beside the other.
explanation.definitionFit: Pirates and buccaneers traditionally carried a short curved sword, so it is the weapon they brandish.

clue.text: Echo upper-class guy, say, being continent

parts.note: Echo is E in the NATO alphabet
U is the old label for upper-class usage
a guy is a rope securing a tent, so it is an example of one

explanation.surface: Copying a posh man who is sexually restrained.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Continent' looks like the adjective meaning self-restrained, but it is the geographical noun; a guy is a tent rope here, not a man.
explanation.definitionFit: Europe is one of the world's large landmasses, so it is an example of the noun.

clue.text: Former power is in decline

parts.note: P is the physics symbol for power
withdrawing, diminishing

explanation.surface: An ex-superpower is fading.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Former power' reads as one phrase, but the definition is the first word alone.
explanation.definitionFit: Both adjectives describe what came earlier in time or order, such as the previous chapter or holder of an office.

clue.text: Episode incorporated channel logo?

parts.note: abbreviation used after American company names
a TV ident is the short clip identifying a broadcaster

explanation.surface: A TV show episode with a broadcaster's branding built into it.
explanation.walkthrough: An ident is British TV jargon for the brief station-identification sequence between programmes; the question mark flags the less familiar term.
explanation.definitionFit: An episode can mean a single event or occurrence in a sequence, which is a synonym for a happening.

clue.text: Doctor harms procedures

parts.note: standard abbreviation
ills as a noun means harms or misfortunes

explanation.surface: A medic whose operations cause injury.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Harms' and 'procedures' both sound like a malpractice story, but each is a plain noun here.
explanation.definitionFit: Fire drills and safety drills are set routines practised in order, so they are established procedures.

clue.text: Pretend pub game left out bubbly often

parts.note: fake

indicators.note: leaving something out means the letter abbreviated from left is dropped

parts.note: pool is a cue game played in bars
L is the abbreviation for left, removed from the game

explanation.surface: Faking a pub game and missing out on the champagne, as often happens.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bubbly' looks like champagne, and 'shampoo' is even old slang for it, but the definition is simply something that is often foamy.
explanation.definitionFit: Hair-washing liquid lathers into foam when used, so it is usually full of suds, which the cryptic description captures.

clue.text: Glib talk by northern model

parts.note: a salesman's smooth patter
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: Smooth chat from a fashion model from the north.
explanation.walkthrough: 'By' only places the pieces side by side; 'model' is not a catwalk figure but a template.
explanation.definitionFit: A template or exemplar to be copied, as a dressmaker's paper guide, so the nouns are synonyms.

clue.text: Drunken spree involving new grooms

indicators.note: to involve is to include, so one letter goes in among the others
a drunk staggers about out of order, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A drunken bender with men about to marry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grooms' suggests bridegrooms on a stag do, but it is a verb meaning tidies oneself.
explanation.definitionFit: A bird smooths its feathers and a person smartens their appearance; both are verbs for tidying oneself up.

clue.text: Spot politician in impressive building

indicators.note: being in something means placed inside it

parts.note: a stately home is a pile
Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: Catching sight of a politician in a grand building.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spot' reads as a verb meaning to see, but it is the noun for a skin blemish.
explanation.definitionFit: A spot on the face is a small inflamed blemish, which is a synonym for this skin bump.

clue.text: Free bar — I need it to get sloshed

indicators.note: letters set free are loosed from their order and can rearrange

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone at an open bar declares they need it to get drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Free bar' looks like a drinks offer, and 'Free' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Sloshed is informal for drunk, which is what the formal adjective means.

clue.text: The best group of Pre-Raphaelites

indicators.note: a group of letters inside a longer word forms the answer

parts.note: the answer runs inside this word

explanation.surface: Praise for the finest artists of the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood.
explanation.walkthrough: The Pre-Raphaelites were a Victorian group of painters, which makes 'group' look like part of the subject.
explanation.definitionFit: A select top tier of people is called the cream, so the noun means the best collectively.

clue.text: Outlet displaying just half of delights

indicators.note: keeping only half means the rest of the word is discarded

parts.note: the first four of its eight letters

explanation.surface: A shop window showing only some of its treats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outlet' means a retail shop here, and the kept half is the front of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: A retail outlet is a shop, and a delicatessen is a shop selling prepared foods, so it is an example.

clue.text: Prison activity

definitions.meaning: second meaning: a commotion or bustle

explanation.walkthrough: Read together it suggests what inmates do all day; the two words are separate meanings of one short word.
explanation.definitionFit: Old slang names jail this way, and the noun also means a flurry of movement or excitement, as in causing a commotion.

clue.text: Returning cheerful about some kind of crude French soldier

indicators.note: about means round, so one piece surrounds another
something returning goes back the way it came

parts.note: feeling up means in good spirits
crude oil, so oil is the kind of crude meant

explanation.surface: A French infantryman coming home happy despite some coarse company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crude' looks like an adjective for vulgar, but as a noun it is unrefined petroleum.
explanation.definitionFit: Poilu, literally hairy one, was the nickname for French infantrymen in the First World War.

clue.text: Cut back rubbish for dress fabric

indicators.note: going back means running the letters the other way

parts.note: a snip is a small cut
nonsense

explanation.surface: Pruning back waste to make material for a dress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut back' reads as trim, but 'back' is the reversal signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Cloth woven with very thin vertical lines is used for suits, so it is a kind of material for clothing.

clue.text: Beginning from envy nice lot spoiled vote

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its first letter

parts.note: first letter

indicators.note: something spoiled is ruined and messed up, so the letters are disordered

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Starting from jealousy, a pleasant crowd ruined their ballot papers.
explanation.walkthrough: A spoiled vote is a ballot paper marked invalid, so 'spoiled' sits naturally beside 'vote'.
explanation.definitionFit: A vote taken to choose representatives or decide an issue is the formal poll, so the nouns are synonyms.

clue.text: Cheerful bride's first fitting

indicators.note: first means the opening letter only

parts.note: first letter
appropriate, proper

explanation.surface: A bride in good spirits at her dress fitting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fitting' looks like a dress fitting but is the adjective meaning appropriate.
explanation.definitionFit: A sunny, lively manner is described both ways, so the adjectives are synonyms for being happy.
